The largest such $m$ is 32. I did not derive this here. It is the value I recall for this competition problem, supported only by a rough sketch of the upper bound, and I did not construct a coloring that attains it.

**Reformulation.** For a red cell, record the pair (number of red cells in its row, number of red cells in its column). The first condition says these pairs are all distinct across red cells.

**Bound sketch.** Take the red cells lying in rows that have exactly $a$ red cells each. If there are $x_a$ such rows, they contain $a x_a$ red cells. These cells all have the same row count $a$, so they must have distinct column counts. Hence $a x_a$ is at most the number $D$ of distinct column-count values that occur.

Two rows with exactly $m$ red cells give $2m \le D$. A rough estimate on how many distinct column counts can fit in a $70\times 70$ table, which I did not carry out in full, suggests $D$ is around 64. That gives $m \le 32$.

ANSWER: 32
